newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy's EMU plans to come under scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Italy's EMU plans to come under scrutiny.

text.p: European Union finance ministers are expected to praise Italy's latest efforts to join a single currency on Monday but will hold back final judgment until a 1998 budget plan is put firmly into place.

The ministerial gathering, which is the first under the Luxembourg EU presidency, will give credit to the Italian government for outlining a rigorous and realistic economic convergence programme that stretches until the year 2000.
"The programme should be well received because of realistic growth assumptions for the underlying economy," said one EU official.
Italy's hopes of joining economic and monetary union in 1999 have been bolstered by growing expectations that the entry criteria for the euro will be applied in a flexible manner.
This judgment stems from the apparent difficulties some large EU economies are having in bringing spending under control this year, in particular France and Germany.
Specifically, the Italian blueprint foresees a budget deficit of 3.0 percent against Gross Domestic Product this year, dipping to 2.8 percent in 1998.
In terms of growth, GDP is expected to advance by 1.2 percent this year and 2.0 percent in 1998.

What still worries many EU officials is the uncertainty over whether the government's budget plan will be fully implemented. In addition, EU ministers are likely to urge Rome to adopt further reforms in the state's pension system.
"The instruments for reaching these figures still have to be put in place," commented another EU official.
EU monetary affairs commissioner, Yves-Thibault de Silguy, has said Italy's defining moment for EMU qualification would come in the autumn when it unveils its 1998 budget.
The emphasis on sustainable budget consolidation has taken on renewed importance given France's admission that its 1997 budget deficit could be significantly higher than three percent of output.
With France considered a critical founding member of EMU, only a lax interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty's criteria would allow the country to enter on schedule.
Importantly, however, there is the presumption among many officials and analysts that any overshooting of the Maastricht target this year would be corrected next year.
Germany, which is also struggling to put its finances in order, has waffled over whether the criterion on budget deficits should be evaluated strictly.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl, seeking to quell an internal political row of the euro's preconditions, recently put his weight firmly behind a strict reading of the deficit target.
Some analysts interpreted Kohl's stance as a pointed message to France to avoid letting its finances deteriorate.
There is also speculation that the hardline stance is a way of regaining a strong bargaining position over which countries might join EMU.
Monday's meeting will also review the results of the Amsterdam summit of EU leaders last month and look forward to an informal meeting of finance ministers in September.
One of the most important issues under the Luxembourg presidency is an evaluation of how best to fix the conversion rates of currencies entering monetary union.
While there are expectations that a definitive plan might emerge over the next six months, Luxembourg monetary officials have tried to play down expectations of a deal.
The informal gathering on September 13 is likely to be the first opportunity for officials to discuss how to maintain currency stability ahead of the euro's introduction.
